lesson.title: Time Base: Turning the Oscilloscope Screen Into a Clock
lesson.summary: The time base control sets how many seconds each horizontal division on an oscilloscope screen represents, which is what lets you read a period directly off the display and convert it to frequency.
lesson.body:
An oscilloscope draws a graph of voltage versus time. The vertical axis, which you will meet properly in the next chapter, tells you how big the signal is. The horizontal axis tells you how fast it is changing, and that axis only means something once you know how many seconds are packed into each division of the grid. That is the job of the time base control, usually a knob or menu labeled seconds per division, or more often time per division since most signals of interest move in milliseconds or microseconds rather than whole seconds.

Internally, the scope sweeps its trace across the screen at a steady, known rate, then redraws it over and over so the waveform appears to sit still. When you turn the time base knob, you are not changing the signal at all, you are changing how much time the fixed width of the screen represents. A typical bench scope has ten horizontal divisions across its display, and the time base control usually steps through a one, two, five sequence, for example 1 millisecond per division, then 2, then 5, then 1 millisecond becomes 10 milliseconds, and so on in both directions. Choosing a coarser setting compresses more cycles onto the screen, choosing a finer setting stretches a single cycle out so you can see its details.

This is where the period of a repeating signal, something you already know how to define, becomes something you can read straight off the grid. Suppose the time base is set to 0.5 milliseconds per division, and one complete cycle of the waveform, from one rising edge to the next identical rising edge, spans exactly 4 divisions on the screen. The period is simply the time per division multiplied by the number of divisions the cycle occupies, so T equals 4 divisions times 0.5 milliseconds per division, which is 2 milliseconds. Since frequency is the reciprocal of period, f equals 1 divided by 0.002 seconds, which works out to 500 hertz. Nothing about the capacitors, resistors, or logic inside the scope entered that calculation, it is purely reading the grid correctly and applying the same T equals 1 over f relationship you already use for period and frequency everywhere else.

In practice you want to pick a time base setting that shows somewhere between two and six full cycles. Too coarse a setting and the waveform looks like a dense blur of many overlapping cycles, making it hard to measure any one period accurately. Too fine a setting and you might only see a fraction of a single cycle, which is useful for examining a fast edge or a glitch but useless for reading off the period. Getting comfortable with this trade off, and with the arithmetic of divisions times time per division, is the foundation for every timing measurement you will make with a scope from here on.
